greek: ἐκπίπτοντα [442] γὰρ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν, ἐν ἀκαρεῖ μέν τινι χρόνῳ τὴν γένεσιν ἔχει, τοὐντεῦθεν δὲ ἀναβαίνει μέχρι τῆς ἀκμῆς. ἔστω γὰρ εἰ τύχοι κατὰ δυσκρασίαν τὸ νόσημα, καθ’ ἣν ἡμῖν ἐπιδέδεικται καὶ ὁ πυρετὸς συνιστάμενος. ἀναγκαῖον οὖν ἐπειδὰν πρῶτον ἡ παρὰ φύσιν αὕτη γένηται θερμασία, πυρέττειν τε τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ἐπιτείνεσθαί τε μέχρι τῆς ἀκμῆς τὴν θερμασίαν. οὗ γὰρ οὐκ ἔστι μέρη, πῶς ἂν εἴη γένεσις ἐν χρόνῳ τοῦδε; ταῦτ’ εἴρηταί μοι καὶ κατ’ ἀρχὰς εὐθέως, ἀπήντησά τε πρὸς αὐτὰ, τῶν μετὰ περιψύξεως εἰσβαλλόντων πυρετῶν ἀναμνήσας. ἀλλ’ ἐν μὲν ταῖς περιόδοις αὐτάρκης ἡ ἀπάντησις· εἷς γὰρ τῶν ἐν μέρει καιρῶν καὶ τῇ τάξει πρῶτος ὁ τῆς περιψύξεως τῆς συμπάσης νόσου· γελοιότατον δ’ ἂν εἴη τὸν τοῦ πρώτου παροξυσμοῦ πρῶτον καιρὸν ἀρχὴν ἡγεῖσθαι τοῦ νοσήματος ὅλου. τὸ γάρ τοι χρήσιμον ὁ καιρὸς οὗτος, ὃν ὀνομάζουσιν ἀρχὴν νοσήματος, εἰς τὰ βοηθήματα κέκτηται, καὶ πρὸς τοῦτον ἀποβλέπων εἶπεν· ἀρχομένων τῶν νούσων, ἤν τι δοκέῃ κινέειν, κίνει, ἀκμαζουσῶν δὲ, ἡσυχίαν ἔχειν βέλτιόν ἐστιν.
rendering_1: For falling away [442] from the natural state, they have their coming-to-be in some instant of time, and from there they ascend up to the acme. For let the disease be, say, one consisting in a dyscrasia, in accordance with which, as has been demonstrated by us, fever too is constituted. It is necessary, then, that as soon as this heat contrary to nature first arises, the man is in fever, and that the heat is intensified up to the acme. For of that which has no parts, how could there be a coming-to-be in time? These things were stated by me right at the beginning too, and I replied to them, by recalling the fevers that make their attack with chilling. But in the case of the periods the reply is sufficient; for the time of the chilling is one of the partial times of the whole disease and first in order; but it would be most ridiculous to regard the first time of the first paroxysm as the beginning of the whole disease. For indeed this time, which they name the beginning of the disease, possesses its usefulness with regard to remedies, and looking to this he said: "When diseases are beginning, if anything seems to need moving, move it; but when they are at their acme, it is better to keep quiet."
rendering_2: For, falling away [442] from the natural state, they have their coming-into-being in an instant of time, and from there they ascend up to the peak. But in the case of the periods the answer is sufficient; for the time of the chilling is one of the partial times of the whole disease, and the first in order. It would, however, be most ridiculous to regard the first time of the first paroxysm as the beginning of the whole disease. greek: ὅταν γὰρ πρῶτον αἰσθήσει σαφὴς ἡ παρακμὴ γένηται, τότε τοῖς ἁρμόττουσιν αὐτῇ βοηθήμασι χρώμεθα· [449] μέχρι δ’ ἂν ἀπὸ τῶν ἴσων ἀριθμῶν ἑστήκῃ τὸ μέγεθος τοῦ πυρετοῦ, μέχρι τοσούτου τῷ μεγέθει τῆς ἀκμῆς οἰκεῖα πράττειν προσήκει. κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἐπ’ ὀφθαλμίας καὶ πλευρίτιδος καὶ πάσης φλεγμονῆς ἑκάστου τε τῶν ἄλλων νοσημάτων οἱ καθόλου καιροὶ τὴν τῶν διαφόρων βοηθημάτων ὑπαγορεύουσι χρῆσιν, αἰσθήσει μετρούμενοι. λογικὸν οὖν γίνεται σκέμμα τὸ περὶ τοῦ πλάτους τῆς ἀκμῆς, εἴτε τῶν κατὰ μέρος παροξυσμῶν, εἴτε τῆς ὅλης νόσου τι σκοποῖτο· νυνὶ δὲ οὐ πρόκειταί μοι τὰ τοιαῦτα διαιρεῖν, ὡς οἱ τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι φέροντες πράττουσιν, ὧν εἷς ἐστι καὶ Ἀρχιγένης. ἀναμίγνυσι γὰρ οὗτος ὁ ἀνὴρ ἰατρικωτάταις πραγματείαις ἐνίοτε μὲν ὑπὲρ ὀνομάτων ζήτησιν, ἔστι δὲ ὅτε καὶ περὶ αὐτῶν τῶν πραγμάτων, ἀλλὰ λογικήν· ἡμεῖς δὲ ὥσπερ ἀεὶ τοῦτο ἐφυλαξάμεθα, καὶ νῦν οὕτω πράξομεν, ἐάσαντες ὑπὲρ ἀκμῆς ἑτέροις ζητεῖν, εἴτε ἄχρονός ἐστιν, εἴτε σὺν χρόνῳ τινὶ, τὴν χρείαν μετρήσομεν αὐτῆς, τὴν φύσιν ὁρῶντες ἐναργῶς ἔν τε ταῖς ἡλικίαις τὴν ἀκμαστικὴν ἐν πλατεῖ χρόνῳ διαλυομένην, ἔν τε τοῖς νοσήμασιν ἐνίοτε μὲν ἐν μακροτέρῳ, πολλάκις δ’ ἐν ἐλάττονι, πάντως δ’ οὖν ἐν αἰσθητῷ.
rendering_1: For as soon as the decline first becomes clear to perception, we then use the remedies suited to it; [449] but so long as the magnitude of the fever stands at the same numbers, for so long it is proper to do what belongs to the magnitude of the peak. In the same way, in ophthalmia, pleuritis, every inflammation and each of the other diseases, the general periods, measured by perception, dictate the use of the different remedies. The inquiry into the breadth of the peak is therefore a logical one, whether one is considering something about the particular paroxysms or about the whole disease. But it is not my present purpose to distinguish such matters, as those do who bring everything into everything, among whom is Archigenes. For this man mixes into the most strictly medical treatises sometimes an inquiry about names, and at times also one about the things themselves, but a logical one. We, just as we have always guarded against this, shall do so now as well. Leaving it to others to inquire about the peak, whether it is timeless or occupies some time, we shall measure its use. For we see its nature plainly: among the ages of life, the age of prime runs its course over a broad span of time, and in diseases the peak runs its course sometimes over a longer span, often over a shorter one, but in every case over a perceptible one.
rendering_2: For when the decline first becomes clear to perception, then we employ the remedies that suit it; [449] but so long as the magnitude of the fever stands at equal measures (ἀπὸ τῶν ἴσων ἀριθμῶν), for so long it is fitting to do what is proper to the magnitude of the acme. In the same way, in ophthalmia and pleuritis and every inflammation and each of the other diseases, the general periods dictate the use of the different remedies, being measured by perception. The inquiry about the breadth of the acme, then, becomes a logical one, whether one were to examine it with regard to the particular paroxysms or with regard to the whole disease; but at present it is not my purpose to draw distinctions about such matters, as those do who bring everything into everything, one of whom is Archigenes. For this man mixes into the most strictly medical treatises sometimes an inquiry about names, and sometimes one about the things themselves, but a logical one; whereas we, just as we have always guarded against this, shall act in the same way now too: leaving it to others to inquire about the acme, whether it is without duration or with some duration, we shall measure its usefulness, seeing clearly that the acmastic nature, both in the ages of life, is dissolved over a broad span of time, and in diseases sometimes over a longer, often over a shorter, but in any case over a perceptible one.

greek: διττὴ δέ ἐστιν αὐτῶν ἡ φύσις· ἔνια μὲν γὰρ αὐτῶν ἔχει τὴν κατασκευὴν, ﻿ [455] ὅταν ἀκριβῶς αὐτὴν ἔχῃ συμπληρουμένην· ἔνια δὲ ἐκ μὲν τῆς τῶν λυομένων ἐστὶ φύσεως, ἀλλ’ ὅταν ἀποκτεῖναι φθάσῃ, κατὰ τοῦτο αὐτοῖς γίνεσθαι συμβαίνει. τριττὸς δὲ καὶ τούτων ὁ τρόπος ἐστίν· ἢ γὰρ διὰ τὴν τοῦ κάμνοντος ἀδυναμίαν, ἢ διὰ τὴν τῶν νοσημάτων ἰσχὺν, ἢ διὰ τὰ συναμφότερα ἀναιρεῖ πρὶν λυθῆναι. καθ’ ἕτερον δὲ λόγον εἷς καινὸς τύπος ἁπάντων ἐστὶ τῶν τοιούτων, ὅταν ὑπὲρ τὴν δύναμιν ᾖ· τὸ γάρ τοι συνέχον αὐτὸ τῆς ἀπωλείας τοῦ κάμνοντος ἐν τούτῳ τέτακται, μήτε σωθῆναι δυναμένου τινὸς, εἰ μὴ κρατήσειεν ἡ φύσις τῆς νόσου, μήτε ἀπόλλυσθαι χωρὶς τοῦ νικηθῆναι μὲν τὴν φύσιν, ἐπικρατέστερον δὲ αὐτῆς γενέσθαι τὸ νόσημα. καὶ διὰ τοῦτό γέ τινες ἓν σημαίνεσθαι νομίζουσιν ἐκ τοῦ μεγάλου νοσήματος, ἐν τῷ πρός τι συνισταμένου, οὐκ εἰδότες ὅτι λέγεται μέν ποτε καὶ οὕτω τὸ μέγα νόσημα, καθάπερ ἂν εἰ καὶ μεῖζον ἐλέγομεν, ὅταν ὑπὲρ τὴν δύναμιν ᾖ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ κατ’ ἰδίαν οὐσίαν, ὡς ἄνθρωπος, ἢ ἵππος, ἢ βοῦς μέγας.
rendering_1: Their nature is twofold. For some of them have the constitution [sc. of fatal diseases?] [455] whenever they have it brought exactly to completion; others are of the nature of those that are resolved, but when [the disease] kills first, it is in this respect that this happens to them. And of these too the manner is threefold: for they carry off [the patient] before being resolved either because of the patient's want of strength, or because of the strength of the diseases, or because of both together. But on another account there is one common pattern for all such cases, namely when [the disease] is beyond the strength. For the very cause that sustains the patient's destruction is set in this: no one can be saved unless nature masters the disease, nor perish without nature being defeated and the disease becoming more powerful than it. And for this reason some think that a single thing is signified by 'great disease', as though it consisted in a relation to something. They do not know that 'great disease' is sometimes said in this way, just as if we were also to say 'greater', when it is beyond the strength. But it is also said with reference to its own proper substance, as a man, or a horse, or an ox is called great.
rendering_2: Their nature is twofold. For some of them have their constitution, [455] when they have it completely brought to fulfilment; others belong to the nature of diseases that are resolved, but when they succeed in killing first, it happens to them in this respect [not to be resolved]. And of these too the manner is threefold: for either on account of the weakness of the patient, or on account of the strength of the diseases, or on account of both together, it destroys [the patient] before being resolved. But on another account there is one common type of all such cases, when it is beyond the capacity [of the patient]; for indeed the very thing that holds together the destruction of the patient is placed in this: that no one can be saved unless nature prevails over the disease, nor perish without nature being defeated and the disease becoming the stronger over it. And for this very reason some suppose that one single thing is signified by 'great disease', it being constituted in the category of relation, not knowing that 'great disease' is indeed sometimes said in this way too, just as if we were to say 'greater', when it is beyond the capacity; but it is also said in respect of its own substance, as a man, or a horse, or an ox is great.

greek: ὡσαύτως δὲ κᾀκεῖνο λέλεκται αὐτῷ· [443] περὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰ τέλεα πάντα ἀσθενέστερα. καὶ μέντοι καὶ τὸ περὶ φαρμακείας εἰρημένον, ὡς πέπονα χρὴ φαρμακεύειν καὶ κινέειν, μὴ ὠμὰ, μηδὲ ἐν ἀρχῇσιν, ἢν μὴ ὀργᾷ. καὶ πρὸς τούτοις γε ἔτι τὸ, ἐν τοῖσιν ὀξέσι πάθεσιν ὀλιγάκις καὶ ἐν ἀρχῇσι τῇσι φαρμακείῃσι χρέεσθαι· πολλά τε πρὸς τούτοις ἕτερα, τὰ μὲν Ἱπποκράτει, τὰ δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἰατροῖς ἅπασι τοῖς παλαιοῖς εἰρημένα, τὴν ἀρχὴν ἡμᾶς οὐκ ἐπιτρέπει νοεῖν τοῦ πρώτου παροξυσμοῦ τὴν εἰσβολὴν, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ μακροτέρου, ὡς καὶ φλεβοτομῆσαι δύνασθαι, καὶ κλυστηρίῳ χρήσασθαι, ποτὲ δὲ εἰ κατεπείγει, καὶ καθῆραι, πρὸς τῷ καὶ γελοῖον εἶναι τῶν ἐντὸς τῆς ἑβδόμης ἡμέρας λυομένων νοσημάτων καὶ τῶν εἰς ἐνιαυτὸν παραμενόντων, ὥσπερ καὶ ὁ τεταρταῖος ἔστιν ὅτε, τὴν ἴσην ἀρχὴν τίθεσθαι. πολλὰ μὲν οὖν εἴρηταί μοι περὶ τῆσδε τῆς ἀρχῆς καὶ κατὰ τὸ περὶ κρίσεων πρῶτον, ἐπιδεικνύντι τὸν πρῶτον τοῦτον καιρὸν ὡς ἄν τις γνωρίσειεν. ἦν δ’ αὐτοῦ κεφάλαιον ἡ ἀπεψία τῆς νόσου. βέλτιον δὲ κᾀνταῦθα πρὸς ἐκείνοις εἰπεῖν, ὅσα τῇ παρούσῃ διεξόδῳ χρήσιμα.
rendering_1: In the same way he has also said this: [443] 'About the beginnings and the ends all things are weaker.' And moreover there is also what is said about purgation, that one should purge and set in motion what is concocted, not what is raw, nor at the beginnings, unless there is turgescence. And in addition to these there is further the saying, 'In acute affections use purgative medicines rarely and at the beginnings.' These, and many other things besides, said some by Hippocrates and others by all the other ancient physicians, do not permit us to understand the beginning as the onset of the first paroxysm. They require us to take it as extending over a longer span, long enough that one can perform phlebotomy and use a clyster, and sometimes, if it is urgent, also purge. Besides, it would be ridiculous to posit an equal beginning for diseases that are resolved within the seventh day and for those that persist for a year, as the quartan sometimes does. Much, then, has been said by me about this beginning also in the first book On Crises, where I showed how one might recognise this first period. Its chief point was the unconcoctedness of the disease. But it is better here too to say, in addition to those things, whatever is useful for the present exposition.
rendering_2: And likewise that too has been said by him: [443] "Around the beginnings and the ends all things are weaker." And indeed also what has been said about purging by drugs, that one must purge and move what is concocted, not what is crude, nor at the beginnings, unless it is in turgescence. And in addition to these, further, the saying: "In acute affections use purging drugs rarely, and at the beginnings." And many other things besides these, some said by Hippocrates, some by all the other ancient physicians, do not permit us to understand the beginning as the onset of the first paroxysm, but as extending over a longer time, such that one is able both to let blood and to use a clyster, and sometimes, if it is urgent, also to purge—in addition to its being ridiculous to posit the same beginning for the diseases that are resolved within the seventh day and for those that persist for a year, as the quartan sometimes does. Many things, then, have been said by me about this beginning also in the first book of On Crises, where I showed how one might recognize this first period; and its chief point was the lack of concoction of the disease. But it is better here too to say, in addition to those things, whatever is useful for the present exposition.

greek: ἑκάστου τῶν νοσημάτων ἴδιός ἐστι χρόνος ὁ τῆς γενέσεως, ἐνίοτε μὲν αἰσθητὸς, ἐνίοτε δὲ οὐκ αἰσθητός· ἀφ’ οὗ πάλιν ὁ τῆς αὐξήσεως οὐχ ὁμοίως ἐπὶ [454] πάντων αἰσθητὸς οὐδὲ οὗ τος· οἷς ὁ τῆς ἀκμῆς ἕπεται πάντως αἰσθητὸς, ὁμολογούντων ἡμῶν ἔστιν ὅτε μηδὲν ἔχειν ἐναργὲς γνώρισμα τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ πάθους καὶ τῆς αὐξήσεως. ἐπὶ τούτων οὖν, ὡς πρὸς τὴν χρείαν τῆς τέχνης, ἀληθῶς τις ἐρεῖ τὸν τῆς ἀκμῆς μόνον ὑπάρχειν καιρόν· εἰ δὲ καὶ σώζεσθαι μέλλοιεν, ἕπεσθαι πάντως αὐτῷ τὸν τῆς παρακμῆς, αἰσθητὸν καὶ τοιοῦτον, ὡς ἂν ἐν χρόνῳ συνιστάμενον οὐκ ἀπλατεῖ. καὶ γὰρ εἰ ἢ δι’ αἱμοῤῥαγίας, ἢ δι’ ἱδρώτων τις ὀξέως κριθείη, χρόνος γοῦν τις ὑπάρχει καὶ τούτῳ αἰσθητὸς ὁ τῆς παρακμῆς· εἰ δ’ ἐλάττονος τούτου καθ’ ἕτερα νοσήματα γινομένου, τρισὶν ἢ τέτταρσιν ἢ καὶ πλέοσιν ἡμέραις παρακμάζοντος, τοῦτο οὐδὲν τὸν ἔμπροσθεν λόγον φαίνεται παραβλάπτον, οὐδὲ διαβάλλει τὸ κεφάλαιον τῆς ἀποφάσεως, ἀλλ’ ἔτι μένει, τὸ πάντων τῶν νοσημάτων, ὅσα λύεται, καθάπερ ἀκμὴν, οὕτω δὴ καὶ παρακμὴν ὑπάρχειν τινά. Τούτων ἡμῖν αὐτάρκως ἀποδεικνυμένων, ἐπισκεψόμεθα περὶ τῶν μὴ λυομένων νοσημάτων.
rendering_1: Each of the diseases has its own proper period of origination, sometimes perceptible, sometimes not perceptible; after which, in turn, the period of increase is not perceptible in the same way in [454] all cases, not even this one. These are followed by the period of the peak, which is in every case perceptible, although we grant that sometimes there is no clear mark of the beginning of the affection and of its increase. In these cases, then, so far as the use of the art is concerned, one will truly say that only the time of the peak exists; and, if the patients are going to be saved, that the period of the decline necessarily follows it, and this too is perceptible, since it is constituted in a time that is not without extension. For even if someone has an acute crisis, whether through a haemorrhage or through sweats, there is at any rate some period of decline in this case too, and a perceptible one. And if in other diseases this occurs to a lesser degree, the disease declining over three or four or even more days, this plainly does no harm to the preceding argument, nor does it discredit the chief point of the assertion; rather, it still stands that all diseases that are resolved have, just as a peak, so also some decline. These things having been sufficiently demonstrated by us, we shall next examine the diseases that are not resolved.
rendering_2: For each of the diseases there is a proper period, that of its generation, sometimes perceptible, sometimes not perceptible; after which, in turn, comes that of the increase, and this too is not perceptible in all cases alike; [454] upon which there follows that of the acme, which is perceptible in every case, while we admit that sometimes we have no clear sign of the beginning of the affection and of its increase. In these cases, then, so far as concerns the use of the art, one will truly say that only the period of the acme exists; but if the patients are also going to be saved, the period of the decline follows upon it in every case, perceptible, and such as to be constituted in a time that is not without breadth (οὐκ ἀπλατεῖ). For even if someone should be brought to crisis swiftly either through hemorrhage or through sweats, there is at any rate for this person too some perceptible period, that of the decline; and if this is shorter than that which occurs in other diseases, which decline over three or four or even more days, this evidently in no way harms the preceding argument, nor does it discredit the chief point of the assertion, but it still stands: that in all diseases which are resolved there is, just as an acme, so also some decline. These matters having been sufficiently demonstrated by us, we shall next examine the diseases which are not resolved.

greek: [440] ΓΑΛΗΝΟΥ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΟΛΟΥ ΤΟΥ ΝΟΣΗΜΑΤΟς ΚΑΙΡΩΝ ΒΙΒΛΙΟΝ. Ὅλου τοίνυν τοῦ νοσήματος ἐπινοοῦμεν καιροὺς ἀνάλογον ταῖς ἡλικίαις τῶν ζώων· ἕνα μὲν καὶ πρῶτον τῆς γενέσεως αὐτοῦ· δεύτερον δὲ τὸν τῆς ἀναβάσεως· τρίτον δὲ τὸν τῆς ἀκμῆς· καὶ τέταρτον τὸν τῆς παρακμῆς, ὅταν γε μέλλωσιν οἱ κάμνοντες σώζεσθαι· φθασάντων γὰρ ἀποθανεῖν αὐτῶν, ἤτοι κατὰ τὴν ἀνάβασιν, ἢ τὴν ἀκμὴν, εὔδηλον ὡς οὐ διεξῆλθεν ἅπαντας τοὺς καιροὺς ἡ τοιαύτη νόσος.
rendering_1: [440] GALEN'S BOOK ON THE PERIODS OF THE WHOLE DISEASE. Of the whole disease, then, we conceive periods analogous to the ages of living beings: one, the first, that of its genesis; the second, that of its increase; the third, that of its peak; and the fourth, that of its decline, at least when the patients are going to be saved. For if they die before this, either during the increase or at the peak, it is quite clear that such a disease has not passed through all the periods.
rendering_2: [440] GALEN'S BOOK ON THE PERIODS OF THE WHOLE DISEASE. Of the whole disease, then, we conceive periods analogous to the ages of living beings: one, and the first, that of its generation; a second, that of its increase; a third, that of its acme; and a fourth, that of its decline, at any rate whenever the patients are going to be saved; for if they have died first, either during the increase or the acme, it is quite evident that such a disease has not passed through all the periods.

greek: καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ἔνια δοκεῖ τῶν νοσημάτων εὐθὺς εἰσβάλλειν ἀκμάζοντά· καὶ τοῦτο μὲν αὐτὸ τῶν ἀδυνάτων ἐστὶν, οὔτε [451] γὰρ ὁ λεγόμενος σύνοχος πυρετὸς εὐθὺς ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκμῆς ποτε εἰσέβαλεν, ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ τῆς πρώτης προσβολῆς ἄχρι τῆς τελεωτάτης ἀκμῆς ὥραις ἤτοι τέτταρσιν ἢ τρισὶν ἀφικνεῖται τοὐλάχιστον, ἐντεῦθεν δὲ πάντως ἴσος ἑαυτῷ μένων συνεχῶς ἄχρι κρίσεως. ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τὸ μάλιστα ἐξαίφνης εἰσβάλλον ἀκμάζον εἴποι τις ἂν, τὴν ἀποπληξίαν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀκριβῶς ἐστι τὸ τοιοῦτον, ἀλλ’ ἐν μὲν βραχεῖ χρόνῳ διεξέρχεται τήν τε ἀρχὴν καὶ τὴν ἀνάβασιν, οὐ μὴν ἄναρχόν γέ ἐστιν, οὐδ’ εὐθὺς εἰσβάλλει τελεώτατα, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ ὁ τῆς ἐπιληψίας παροξυσμός· οὐδεὶς γὰρ οὕτως ἁλίσκεται ἐξαίφνης τῷ συμπτώματι, καθάπερ οἱ τὸν τράχηλον ἀφαιρούμενοι, καίτοι καὶ τούτων ἡ τομὴ πρῶτόν τινα χρόνον ἔχει καὶ δεύτερον καὶ τρίτον καὶ τέταρτον, ὥσπερ εἰ καὶ χειρουργός τις ὁτιοῦν τέμνοι. ἀλλὰ γὰρ, εἰ βούλει, συγχωρείσθω χωρὶς χρόνου τήν τε ἐπιληπτικὴν καὶ τὴν ἀποπληκτικὴν γίνεσθαι κατάπτωσιν, ἵν’ ὅ γε ἐξ ἀρχῆς προὐθέμην διέλθω.
rendering_1: And on this account some diseases seem to attack at once at their peak. Yet this very thing is among the impossibilities; for [451] not even the so-called synochus fever ever attacked straight from its peak; rather, from the first onset it reaches its most complete peak in four or three hours at the least, and from that point it remains entirely equal to itself, continuously, until the crisis. Nor would one say that the disease which attacks most suddenly of all, apoplexy, is at its peak; for such is not strictly the case. In a short time it passes through both the beginning and the ascent, yet it is certainly not without a beginning, nor does it attack at once in its most complete form, just as the paroxysm of epilepsy does not either. For no one is seized by the symptom as suddenly as those who have their neck severed; and yet even in their case the cutting has a first period of time, and a second, a third and a fourth, just as when a surgeon cuts anything whatever. But, if you wish, let it be granted that both the epileptic and the apoplectic falling-down occur without time, so that I may go through what I proposed at the outset.
rendering_2: And on this account some diseases seem to attack at once at their acme; yet this very thing is among the impossibilities, for not even [451] the so-called synochos (continuous) fever ever attacked immediately from its acme, but from the first onset to the most complete acme it arrives in four or three hours at the very least, and from then on it remains altogether equal to itself continuously until the crisis. But neither could one say that what attacks most suddenly of all, apoplexy, attacks at its acme; for such a thing is not strictly the case, but rather it passes through its beginning and its increase in a short time; yet it is not without a beginning, nor does it attack at once in its most complete form, just as neither does the paroxysm of epilepsy. For no one is seized so suddenly by the symptom as those who have their neck cut off; and yet even in their case the cut has a first portion of time and a second and a third and a fourth, just as if some surgeon were cutting anything whatever. But still, if you wish, let it be granted that the epileptic and the apoplectic collapse occur without time, so that I may go through what I set out from the beginning.

greek: [448] Περὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων, ἐν οἷς ἀπόλλυνται, μικρὸν ὕστερον ἐρῶ, διαρθρώσας πρότερον, ὅσα διορισμοῦ τινος τῶν εἰρημένων δέονται. ἓν μὲν οὖν ἐστιν αὐτῶν καὶ τὸ περὶ τῆς ἀκμῆς, εἴτε ἄχρονος ὑπάρχει διαπαντὸς, ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῇ, κᾂν εἰ πρὸς τὴν αἴσθησιν φαίνοιτο παρεκτεινομένη πολλάκις ἀξιολόγοις χρόνοις· εἴτε διαπαντὸς ἔχει τι πλάτος, ὁτὲ μὲν μεῖζον, ὁτὲ δὲ ἔλαττον· εἴτ’ ἐπὶ τινῶν μὲν νοσημάτων ἔγχρονος, ἐπὶ τινῶν δὲ ἄχρονος. μακροτέρου δὲ λόγου δεομένου τοῦ σκέμματος, ἔοικα παραλείψειν αὐτὸν ἅπαντα, μιμησάμενος Ἱπποκράτη περὶ τῆς κατὰ τὸν ὦμον ἐκπτώσεως εἰπόντα· οὐ μέντοι ἰσχυρίζω ἔγωγε περὶ αὐτοῦ, καίτοι ἔχων ὅ τι λέγω. καθάπερ γὰρ ἐκεῖνος ἠρκέσθη τοῖς διαπαντὸς ἑωραμένοις αὐτῷ, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον κᾀγὼ νῦν ὡς διαπαντὸς ἰδὼν ἐρῶ. πᾶσαν ἀκμὴν τῶν κατὰ μέρος παροξυσμῶν χρόνῳ γινομένην ἐθεασάμην, ὥστε κᾂν εἰ πρὸς τὴν φύσιν ἄχρονος εἴη, μηδεμιᾶς ἐξ αὐτοῦ χρείας ἀπολαύειν ἡμᾶς.
rendering_1: [448] As for the other times, those in which patients perish, I shall speak of them a little later, after first articulating whatever of what has been said requires some qualification. One of these is the question concerning the peak: whether it is always without duration, so far as it itself is concerned, even if to perception it often appears to be extended over considerable periods of time; or whether it always has some breadth, sometimes greater and sometimes less; or whether in some diseases it occupies a span of time and in others is without duration. But since the inquiry requires a longer discussion, I am inclined to pass over the whole of it, imitating Hippocrates, who said concerning dislocation at the shoulder: 'I do not, however, insist on this myself, although I have something to say.' For just as he was content with what he had always seen, in the same way I too shall now speak as one who has always seen it. Every peak of the individual paroxysms I have observed to take place over a span of time, so that even if by its nature it were without duration, we would derive no use from that fact.
rendering_2: [448] Concerning the others, in which the patients perish, I shall speak a little later, having first articulated those of the things said which require some distinction. One of these, then, is also the question concerning the acme: whether it is always without duration, so far as depends on itself, even if to perception it often appears to be extended over considerable periods of time; or whether it always has some breadth, at one time greater, at another less; or whether in some diseases it has duration, while in others it is without duration. But since the inquiry requires a longer discussion, I am inclined to pass over it entirely, imitating Hippocrates, who said concerning the dislocation at the shoulder: "I, for my part, do not insist upon this, although I have something I could say." For just as he was content with what he had always observed, in the same way I too shall now speak as one who has always seen it so. I have observed every acme of the individual paroxysms to come about over a period of time, so that even if with respect to its nature it were without duration, we derive no use from that fact.

greek: ἐπινόησον τοίνυν, οὐ γὰρ ἀδύνατον, ἐν τοῖς σιμοῖς τοῦ ἥπατος ἤδη τινὰ ὄγκον συνίστασθαι σκιῤῥώδη· καὶ λήσεται μέχρι τινὸς τούτου ἡ σύστασις, ὕστερον μέντοι τὰ τῆς διαθέσεως αὐτῆς ἔσται φανερώτερα, μηδὲ τότε δυναμένων ἡμῶν ἐξευρεῖν, ἐφ’ ᾗ διαθέσει τοῦτο συμβαίνει· χρόνῳ δὲ ὕστερον ἤδη που καὶ παρέγχυσις ὑδερικὴ [453] συμβήσεται, μηδὲ τότε πρὸς τὴν ἁφὴν διασημαίνοντος τοῦ σκιῤῥώδους ὄγκου· ἀλλ’ ὕστερόν γε φανεὶς ἀξιόλογος ἀνέμνησεν ἡμᾶς τῆς ἔμπροσθεν ἀγνοίας. οὐκ ὀλίγους γοῦν ἐγὼ τεθέαμαι κατὰ τὴν τοιαύτην ὁδὸν τῶν συμπτωμάτων ἐν ὀλίγῳ χρόνῳ προφήναντας ὄγκον οὐ σμικρὸν ἐν ἥπατι σκιῤῥώδει, συνιστάμενον μὲν ἐκ πολλοῦ, λανθάνοντα δὲ διὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ σμικρότητα καὶ εὐτροφίαν τῶν καθ’ ὑποχόνδριον μυῶν. ἀλλ’ ὅταν αὐξανόμενος ὁ σκίῤῥος ἅμα μὲν ἐπαναβῇ τοῖς κύρτοις τοῦ ἥπατος, ἅμα δὲ ἀτροφίας αἴτιος γένηται τοῖς τε ἄλλοις τοῦ ζώου μορίοις καὶ τοῖς καθ’ ὑποχόνδριον μυσὶν, ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων τούτων ἐναργῶς ἐν ὀλίγῳ χρόνῳ διαγνώσεις, αὐτοῦ ἤδη ὑπάρξαντος ἀξιολόγου μεγέθους. τὰ μὲν δὴ τοιαῦτα πάντα συνῆπται τῇ τῶν πεπονθότων μορίων ἐπισκέψει, περὶ ἧς οὐ πρόκειται μὲν ἐν τῷ παρόντι σκοπεῖσθαι, δεδήλωται δὲ ὑπὲρ τῆς κοινωνίας αὐτῶν οὐκ ἀχρήστως. ἐπὶ δὲ τὸν ἐξ ἀρχῆς λόγον ἰέναι καιρός.
rendering_1: Conceive, then (for it is not impossible), that some scirrhous swelling is already forming in the concave parts of the liver. Its formation will escape notice up to a certain point. Later, however, the features of the condition itself will become more evident, though even then we are unable to discover upon what condition this ensues. At a still later time a dropsical effusion [453] will at some point also occur, while even then the scirrhous swelling gives no distinct sign to the touch. But having later become manifest, and of considerable size, it reminded us of our earlier ignorance. At any rate, I myself have seen not a few patients who, by such a course of the symptoms, showed within a short time a swelling of no small size in a scirrhous liver. It had been forming for a long time but escaped notice because of its own smallness and the good nourishment of the muscles in the hypochondrium. But when the scirrhus, as it grows, at once mounts up onto the convex parts of the liver and at the same time becomes a cause of lack of nourishment both to the other parts of the animal and to the muscles in the hypochondrium, then from both of these you will clearly diagnose it within a short time, since it has by then reached a considerable size. All such matters belong to the inquiry into the affected parts, which it is not our present purpose to examine; but they have been set out, not without use, because of their connection with it. It is time to return to the original argument.
rendering_2: Conceive, then—for it is not impossible—that in the concave parts of the liver some scirrhous tumour is already forming; and its formation will escape notice up to a certain point, though later the features of the disposition itself will become more evident, while not even then are we able to discover in what disposition this occurs; and some time later, at some point, a hydropic effusion [453] will also supervene, the scirrhous tumour not even then giving any indication to the touch; but later at least, having appeared of notable size, it reminded us of our previous ignorance. At any rate I have seen not a few who, along such a course of symptoms, in a short time brought to light a not small tumour in a scirrhous liver, one that had been forming for a long time but had escaped notice on account of its smallness and the good nourishment of the muscles in the hypochondrium. But when the scirrhus, as it grows, at once mounts up to the convex parts of the liver and at the same time becomes the cause of atrophy both to the other parts of the animal and to the muscles in the hypochondrium, from both of these you will clearly diagnose it in a short time, it having already attained a notable size. All such matters, indeed, are connected with the examination of the affected parts, which it is not our purpose to investigate at present, but what has been shown concerning their association has not been without use. But it is time to go on to the argument from the beginning.

greek: τὸ μὲν οὖν εὔχροον οὖρον καὶ μετρίως παχὺ πάντων οὔρων ἐστὶ κάλλιστον, ὅσον ἐπὶ τῇ χροιᾷ καὶ συστάσει· συμπαρεῖναι δὲ αὐτῷ χρὴ πάντως ἤτοι γε ἐναιώρημα χρηστὸν, [457] ἢ νεφέλην, ἢ ὑπόστασιν, ὡς ἂν ἡ τοῦ νοσήματος ἀπαιτῇ φύσις· ἄλλως μὲν γὰρ ἐδείξαμεν ἐν τοῖς χολώδεσι νοσήμασιν, ἄλλως δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἐξ ὠμῶν χυμῶν πλήθεσι τὰς ὑποστάσεις γινομένας. ἐκ διαμέτρου δὲ, ὡς ἄν τις εἴποι, τὸ μὲν ἄπεπτον οὖρόν ἐστιν, ὃ μήτε ἐναιώρημα μήτε ὑπόστασιν ἔχει μήτε νεφέλην, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ πάχος τι προσειληφὸς, ἢ ὠχρότητα, λευκὸν δέ ἐστι τῇ χροιᾷ, καὶ λεπτὸν τῇ συστάσει, καθάπερ ὕδωρ· εἰ μέντοι νεφέλη τις, ἢ ἐναιώρημα μέλαν, ἢ ὑπόστασις ἐν αὐτῷ γένοιτο μέλαινα, καὶ μᾶλλον εἰ καὶ σύμπαν εἴη ζοφῶδες, ὀλέθριον ὑπάρχει· καθάπερ εἰ καὶ κριμνώδη τινὰ, ἢ πεταλώδη κατ’ αὐτὸ φαίνοιτο· καὶ μὴν καὶ τὸ δυσῶδες ἰσχυρῶς, καὶ τὸ λιπαρὸν, ὅπερ ἐλαιῶδες ὀνομάζουσιν, ὀλέθριον. ταῦτα οὖν ἐστι τὰ οὖρα, μεγάλου νοσήματος γνωρίσματα, ὃ κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φύσιν ἔλεγον ὑπάρχειν μέγα.
rendering_1: Well-coloured urine, then, that is moderately thick is the finest of all urines, so far as colour and consistency are concerned; but there must in every case be present along with it either a good suspended matter (enaiōrēma), [457] or a cloud, or a sediment, as the nature of the disease demands; for we showed that the sediments come about in one way in bilious diseases and in another in the plethoras arising from crude humours. Diametrically opposite, as one might say, is the unconcocted urine, which has neither suspended matter nor sediment nor cloud, and which, moreover, has not taken on any thickness or yellowness, but is white in colour and thin in consistency, like water; if, however, some black cloud, or black suspended matter, or black sediment should arise in it, and still more if the whole of it should be dusky, it is deadly; just as also if bran-like or scale-like particles should appear in it; and indeed, urine that is strongly foul-smelling, and that which is fatty, which they call oily, is deadly. These, then, are the urines that are marks of a great disease, one which, I was saying, is great according to its own nature.
rendering_2: Now the urine that is of good colour and moderately thick is the finest of all urines, so far as colour and consistency are concerned. But there must by all means be present together with it either a favourable suspended matter, [457] or a cloud, or a sediment, as the nature of the disease may demand. For we have shown that sediments come about in one way in bilious diseases and in another way in plethoras arising from crude humours. At the diametrically opposite extreme, as one might say, is the unconcocted urine, which has neither suspended matter nor sediment nor cloud, and has not even taken on any thickness or yellowness, but is white in colour and thin in consistency, like water. If, however, some cloud, or a black suspended matter, or a black sediment should form in it, and still more if the whole of it should be murky, it is deadly; just as it is also if things like coarse meal or like flakes should appear in it. And indeed urine that is strongly foul-smelling is also deadly, and so is the greasy urine, which they call oily. These, then, are the urines that are distinguishing marks of a great disease, that is, of one which, as I was saying, is great by its own nature.
